mcqs.question: A class `Foo` is referenced as `Foo.class` but its static method is never called. Has `Foo` been initialized?
options: Yes — referencing a class in any form triggers full initialization
No — merely referencing the class doesn't trigger initialization; that happens on active use, such as calling a static method
Only if `Foo` has no static fields
Only if `Foo` was loaded by the bootstrap classloader
mcqs.explanation: Initialization (running static initializers) is deferred until the class is actively used, not merely mentioned — this is why NoClassDefFoundError-style issues can surface later than where a class first appears. It doesn't depend on the presence of static fields or which classloader loaded it.

mcqs.question: Why are a thread's local variables automatically safe from other threads without any locking?
options: The JIT automatically synchronizes all local variable access
The JVM copies local variables into the heap for every method call
Local variables live on that thread's own per-thread stack, which no other thread can access
Local variables are immutable by default in Java
mcqs.explanation: Each thread has its own private call stack holding its local variables and frames, so there is nothing for another thread to race with — this is a memory-layout fact, not a synchronization mechanism. Local variables aren't heap-allocated by default, aren't auto-synchronized, and aren't immutable.

mcqs.question: An app throws `OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace` after repeated redeploys in a dev environment. Will increasing `-Xmx` (heap size) fix it?
options: Yes, since heap and metaspace share the same underlying memory pool
No — metaspace holds class metadata, a separate region from the heap, so heap tuning doesn't address a classloader leak
Yes, but only on JVMs older than Java 8
No, because metaspace errors can only be fixed by disabling the garbage collector
mcqs.explanation: Heap and metaspace are distinct memory regions with distinct failure causes; a metaspace leak is almost always classes/classloaders staying reachable across redeploys, which more heap does nothing to fix. The regions aren't shared, JVM version doesn't change this, and disabling GC isn't the remedy either.

mcqs.question: What's the practical difference between HotSpot's C1 and C2 compilers?
options: C1 compiles fast with light optimization and adds profiling instrumentation; C2 compiles slower but far more aggressively, using data C1 collected
C1 is used only for static methods; C2 is used only for instance methods
C1 and C2 produce identical output and only differ in which OS they run on
C2 runs before C1 for every method
mcqs.explanation: C1 is the fast, lightly-optimizing tier that also instruments code to gather better profile data; C2 spends more compile time on aggressive optimizations like inlining and escape analysis, informed by that data. The tiers aren't split by method kind or OS, and interpretation/C1 always precede C2, not the reverse.

mcqs.question: A `-XX:+PrintCompilation` trace shows the same method compiled, then "made not entrant," then recompiled — repeatedly, under real production load. What does this most likely indicate?
options: Normal, harmless JVM behavior with no diagnostic value
The JVM is out of heap memory
Repeated deoptimization, often caused by unstable call-site type patterns worth investigating
The class file on disk is corrupted
mcqs.explanation: "Made not entrant" followed by recompilation is the signature of deoptimization; seeing it recur for the same method under load points to a call site whose observed types keep shifting. It's not routine noise once it recurs, and it has no direct relationship to heap exhaustion or file corruption.

mcqs.question: Metaspace usage climbs with every redeploy of a web app and never shrinks, even though the old code should be garbage. What's the actual root cause?
options: Metaspace is a fixed-size region that can never be reclaimed once allocated
Something — a lingering thread, a static reference, an unclosed driver registration — is still keeping the old classloader (and its whole class graph) reachable
The application server does not support garbage collection for classes
Redeploying always doubles metaspace usage regardless of leaks
mcqs.explanation: This is a reachability problem: metaspace for a classloader can be reclaimed once nothing references it, so a leak means some object outside the redeployed app is still holding a reference, keeping the whole old class graph alive. Metaspace isn't fixed and unreclaimable, class GC does exist, and redeploys don't inherently double usage absent a leak.
